article.title: The Identification Problem: Why Prediction Is Easier Than Knowing What Caused an Outcome
article.why: Practical analytical English with higher-difficulty emphasis.

paragraphs.en:
Prediction and causal inference often use the same variables, models, and datasets, but they answer fundamentally different questions. A prediction problem asks what is likely to happen. A causal problem asks what would happen if we changed something. The gap between those questions is the identification problem: under what assumptions can observed data reveal a causal effect that is not directly observable?

Suppose a company finds that customers who use its mobile app spend more than customers who do not. A prediction model can use app usage as a powerful feature if the association is stable. It does not need to know why the relationship exists. If the business asks whether encouraging app adoption will increase spending, however, the correlation is not enough. Customers who choose the app may already be younger, more digitally engaged, wealthier, or more loyal. Those characteristics can affect both app adoption and spending. The observed difference therefore combines any causal effect of the app with pre-existing differences between users and non-users.

The core difficulty is the counterfactual. For each customer, we can observe spending under the world that actually occurred, but not simultaneously observe spending for the same customer under the alternative world in which app usage was different. Causal inference tries to reconstruct this missing comparison using design and assumptions. Randomized experiments solve much of the identification problem by assigning treatment independently of pre-treatment characteristics in expectation. In observational data, analysts rely on assumptions such as conditional exchangeability, positivity, consistency, or specific structural models.

Confounding is only one threat. Selection can arise when the analysis includes only customers who remain active long enough to be observed. Conditioning on variables affected by treatment can create collider or post-treatment bias. Measurement error can distort both exposure and outcome. Policy rules can determine who receives an offer, approval, or review, making the observed data endogenous to previous decisions.

This is why a sophisticated predictive model does not automatically become a causal model. Gradient boosting, neural networks, or large language models can estimate complex associations extremely well, but causal identification comes primarily from design and assumptions, not algorithmic flexibility. Machine learning can help estimate nuisance functions, heterogeneous effects, or high-dimensional relationships once the causal structure is credible. It cannot recover an effect that the data and assumptions do not identify.

A useful workflow begins by writing the causal question precisely: treatment, outcome, target population, and time horizon. Next, draw or describe the data-generating process and identify possible confounders, mediators, colliders, and selection mechanisms. Then choose a design—randomization, natural experiment, matching, weighting, regression adjustment, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, or another approach—whose assumptions are defensible in context.

Sensitivity analysis is also important. Observational studies rarely eliminate all uncertainty about unmeasured confounding. Rather than presenting one adjusted estimate as unquestionable truth, analysts should explain which assumptions drive identification and how conclusions would change if those assumptions were violated.

The business distinction is practical. Prediction helps allocate attention toward likely outcomes: who may churn, default, buy, or need support. Causal inference helps choose actions: whom to contact, which policy to change, whether an incentive works, or what would happen under a different decision rule. Confusing the two can lead to interventions aimed at people who are easy to predict but difficult to influence. Strong analytics therefore separates ‘who is likely to do X?’ from ‘what action will change X?’ and treats identification as a design problem before it becomes a modeling problem. Identification also determines what can be learned from popular business comparisons. A difference between exposed and unexposed customers, before and after a campaign, or high- and low-usage groups may be descriptively accurate while still failing to identify an intervention effect. The missing ingredient is a credible reason why the comparison represents the counterfactual that would have occurred otherwise.

Different research designs solve different parts of this problem. Difference-in-differences uses changes over time in a comparison group and relies on a form of parallel-trends assumption. Instrumental-variable designs exploit variation that changes treatment but affects the outcome only through that treatment under strong assumptions. Regression discontinuity uses a cutoff rule when units just above and below the threshold are comparable. These methods are powerful precisely because they create or justify a comparison, not because they use more sophisticated prediction algorithms.

Target population matters too. Even a randomized experiment identifies an effect for the population and setting represented by the experiment. If participants are unusually engaged, if treatment implementation differs across regions, or if the market changes later, transporting the result requires additional assumptions. Analysts should separate internal validity—whether the design identifies an effect in the study—from external validity—whether that effect applies elsewhere.

Heterogeneous treatment effects create another practical complication. The average effect can be positive while some customer groups benefit little, receive no benefit, or are harmed. Estimating those differences requires enough information and sample size, careful pre-treatment features, and protection against discovering noisy subgroups. Uplift models and causal forests can help, but only after the underlying treatment assignment and outcome measurement support causal interpretation.

Identification thinking also improves ordinary business conversations. Instead of asking vaguely, ‘Does the app increase sales?’, analysts can ask, ‘For currently eligible customers who are not active app users, what is the 90-day incremental spending effect of an intervention that successfully increases app adoption?’ The more precise question exposes what data and design are required. It may reveal that the company can predict app usage accurately but has never generated variation that identifies the effect of changing it.

This discipline prevents a common failure mode: optimizing interventions using variables that are merely markers of desirable customers. Wealth, loyalty, prior spending, or engagement may be excellent predictors, yet they are not necessarily levers. Causal decision making requires distinguishing signals that tell us who someone is from actions that can change what happens next.
paragraphs.zh:
【擴充翻譯】Prediction 問『接下來最可能發生什麼』，causal inference 問『如果我們改變某件事，結果會怎樣』。兩者真正的差別在 identification：觀察資料在什麼假設下，足以識別一個看不見的 counterfactual effect？例如 app 使用者消費較高，對 prediction 來說 app usage 可以是好 feature；但若要問『推動 app adoption 是否會增加消費』，就必須處理原本就較年輕、數位化、忠誠或高消費的使用者差異。

因果問題的核心是同一個人無法同時被觀察在 treatment 與 no-treatment 兩種世界。RCT 透過隨機化讓比較組在期望上可比；observational study 則必須靠 conditional exchangeability、positivity、consistency 等假設或結構性設計。confounding 只是其中一種威脅；selection、post-treatment conditioning、collider、measurement error 與舊 policy 造成的 endogenous data 都可能破壞 identification。

這也是為什麼 predictive model 再強，也不會自動變成 causal model。gradient boosting 或 neural network 能非常精準地學 association，但 identification 主要來自 research design 與 assumptions。machine learning 可以在設計可信後，幫忙估 nuisance function、heterogeneous treatment effect 或高維關係，卻不能從根本上不存在的 comparison 中創造因果資訊。

不同設計處理不同 identification 問題。difference-in-differences 依賴 parallel trends；instrumental variables 需要 instrument 只透過 treatment 影響 outcome 等強假設；regression discontinuity 利用 cutoff 附近的可比性。它們的價值不是『演算法更高級』，而是提供合理 counterfactual。

實務上先把問題寫清楚：treatment、outcome、target population、time horizon，再畫出 data-generating process，辨認 confounder、mediator、collider 與 selection。也要區分 internal validity 與 external validity，並對未量測 confounding 做 sensitivity analysis。最重要的是把『誰最可能做 X』和『什麼 action 能改變 X』分開，否則容易把資源投向很容易預測、卻根本不容易被影響的人。
paragraphs.ja:
【拡張訳】Predictionは「何が起こりそうか」を問うのに対し、causal inferenceは「何かを変えたらoutcomeがどう変わるか」を問う。両者の差の中心がidentificationである。たとえばapp userの消費が高いというassociationはpredictionには使えるが、「app adoptionを促進すれば消費が増えるか」を答えるには、もともとの年齢、digital engagement、loyalty、所得などの差を扱う必要がある。

因果推論の難しさはcounterfactualにある。同じcustomerについてtreatmentを受けた世界と受けない世界を同時には観察できない。RCTはrandomizationによって比較可能性を作るが、observational dataではconditional exchangeability、positivity、consistencyなどのassumptionやresearch designが必要になる。confoundingだけでなく、selection、post-treatment variable、collider、measurement error、過去policyによるendogeneityもidentificationを壊し得る。

高度なpredictive modelがそのままcausal modelになるわけではない。gradient boostingやneural networkはassociationを柔軟に学習できるが、因果効果を識別できるかは主にdesignとassumptionで決まる。machine learningはcredibleなcausal structureがある後でnuisance functionやheterogeneous effectを推定する助けにはなるが、存在しないcounterfactual comparisonを作り出すことはできない。

difference-in-differences、instrumental variables、regression discontinuityなどは、それぞれ異なる仮定の下で比較を正当化する。重要なのはalgorithmの複雑さではなく、なぜその比較がcounterfactualを表すのかである。実務ではtreatment、outcome、target population、time horizonを明確にし、confounder、mediator、collider、selectionを整理する。そして「誰がXしそうか」と「どのactionがXを変えるか」を分けて考える必要がある。

vocabulary.usage: The core issue of whether a causal effect can be learned from observed data.
A variable affecting both treatment and outcome.
Requires treatment possibilities across relevant covariate patterns.
Conditioning on it can introduce bias.
Describes data shaped by the process being studied.
A design for causal identification under strong assumptions.
Uses a cutoff to create local comparability.
Describes effects that vary across groups.

business.term: Prediction finds likely outcomes; causal inference evaluates actions.
business.explanation: Prediction 找可能發生的事，因果推論評估行動。

business.term: Treat identification as a design problem before a modeling problem.
business.explanation: 先處理識別與設計，再談模型。
